title: The Rise And Fall Of Liberal Democracy’s Shared Fiction | NOEMA
gist: Macario Schettino argues the crisis of liberal democracy is the collapse of a 'transcendent belief' — postwar universal citizenship — triggered not by economics but by the 2006-2011 shift from broadcast television to social media, and formally exposed by JD Vance's Feb. 14, 2025 Munich speech. He frames history as a sequence of communication-technology shocks (printing press, newspapers, radio/film, TV, social media) that each fragmented the public sphere and were then re-stabilized by the mature form of the same technology, predicting AI-shaped platforms will build the next framework over a decades-long, likely violent interregnum.

insights.claim: Large-scale human cooperation depends on collective conviction in 'shared fictions' — money, religions, nations — and political crises are best read as the breakdown of those fictions rather than as policy failures.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Reframes political risk as belief-system risk: shocks that look economic or electoral may be symptoms of a legitimacy substrate eroding, which mean-reverting macro models will miss.
insights.quote: today’s crisis, like others of a similar nature before it, was driven by the breakdown of “shared fictions”
insights.locator: At a deeper level, today’s crisis

insights.claim: Societies specifically organize around 'transcendent beliefs' — faith in something that outlasts individual death — because humans are the only animal that knows it will die and the only one with language complex enough to build permanent collective fictions around that knowledge.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Supplies the author's core diagnostic: any proposed replacement order that offers no answer to mortality and meaning is structurally unstable regardless of its material performance.
insights.quote: We are the only animal that knows it will die, and we are the only animal that has built permanent collective fictions around that knowledge.
insights.locator: Societies organize themselves around a specific kind

insights.claim: The postwar liberal-democratic order is the hardest transcendent frame humans have ever attempted because it offers no comfort — it asks millions of strangers to accept that what unites them is primarily a balance of market prices and votes, with no soul, ancestor or god behind it.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Explains why liberal democracy loses to identity and grievance politics in an attention market: its value proposition is materially strong but emotionally bankrupt, a durable structural disadvantage.
insights.quote: It is the hardest transcendent frame humans have ever tried to inhabit, because it offers no comfort.
insights.locator: This framework has been brittle from the start

themes.theme: From climate shocks to communication shocks

insights.claim: For most of human history the disruptor of belief systems was climate: the end of the last Ice Age produced ancestor worship, the 8.2-ka event produced polytheistic 'small gods' that integrated clans into early cities, and the 4.2-ka event produced moralizing 'Big Gods' that legitimized territorial states and empires.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Gives a base-rate framing: belief-system regime changes are rare, exogenously triggered, and each historically enabled a step-change in the scale of cooperation — i.e., in the size of markets.
insights.quote: climatic shocks were punctuation marks of cultural evolution that destabilized existing social orders and yielded new transcendent belief systems enabling large-scale cooperation
insights.locator: Consider the end of the last Ice Age

insights.claim: Since the 16th century the engine of belief-system disruption switched from climate to communications technology, because collective fictions are built on language — so every new medium forces a redrawing of the transcendent framework.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: The central causal claim: media-platform transitions are the leading indicator of political-order transitions, making communications tech a macro variable rather than a sector.
insights.quote: Because our collective fictions are built on language, new communications technologies imply the need for new fictions.
insights.locator: Again and again, climatic shocks were punctuation marks

insights.claim: Since the printing press, each successive transcendent framework has recentered on the individual rather than the collective — citizenry, nation, class — a directional drift rather than a random walk.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Implies the next framework will also be more granular and individualized, not a return to tribal or national aggregates — a bearish read on national-revival political projects.
insights.locator: Each new medium has forced a redrawing

insights.claim: The printing press caused the first communication-driven order change: Luther's 1517 '95 Theses' were translated and mass-reproduced so hundreds of thousands of pamphlets spread across northern Europe within a generation, faster than the Church could respond.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: The template for viral-distribution asymmetry: incumbents lose because response latency exceeds diffusion speed — the same mechanism now facing legacy institutions.
insights.quote: hundreds of thousands of pamphlets had spread Luther’s arguments across northern Europe faster than the Church could respond
insights.locator: In 1517, the printing press changed everything

insights.claim: Belief-system transitions have historically been catastrophically violent: the religious tensions unleashed by printed Lutheran ideas laid the foundations for the Thirty Years' War, in which roughly a third of Central Europe's population died.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Sets the tail-risk distribution for the current transition — the author explicitly treats mass violence as within the historical range of outcomes, not an outlier.
insights.quote: Roughly a third of the population of Central Europe died in the war.
insights.locator: Not only did the disruptive force change

insights.claim: The 18th-century newspaper-and-coffee-house layer let untrained publics follow arguments in real time, and the 1755 Lisbon earthquake became a public test — divine punishment versus natural disaster — of which transcendent frame would hold, with the Enlightenment emerging as the answer.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Shows how a single salient disaster can act as the forcing event that resolves a contested interpretive regime — worth watching for the modern analogue.
insights.quote: the explanations on offer — divine punishment versus natural disaster — became a public test of which transcendent frame would hold
insights.locator: The second communication-driven shift

insights.claim: Radio and film enabled totalitarianism's specific signature — the manufactured national emotion — because mass media made it possible for one voice to reach millions, running from 'The Birth of a Nation' (1915) through Mussolini's and Hitler's radio speeches to Riefenstahl's and Eisenstein's propaganda films.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Establishes the author's mapping of media architecture to political form — one-to-many centralization yields authoritarianism, which matters for how AI-mediated distribution is regulated.
insights.quote: Mass media made it possible for one voice to reach millions, which in turn made possible totalitarianism’s specific signature: the manufactured national emotion.
insights.locator: The citizen-centered framework stabilized around 1815

insights.claim: Postwar liberal democracy was a television format: a person on a screen reached millions with a handful of simple ideas — employment, wages, taxes, the security state — which parties packaged as platforms and sold at elections, producing the citizen as consumer of national policy choices.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: If the party-platform model was a broadcast artifact, its decay is structural and permanent — political forecasting built on party identity and platform coherence is losing predictive power.
insights.quote: This was the system of postwar liberal democracy: the citizen as consumer of national policy choices.
insights.locator: After the Second World War, television produced

insights.claim: The postwar system began dissolving in 2006 with modern social media platforms, accelerated in 2007 with the smartphone, and ruptured between 2008 and 2011 with the Great Recession — a specific, datable technological rather than economic origin for the crisis.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Dates the regime break to platform launch, not to the financial crisis; implies fiscal or monetary fixes cannot restore political stability because the transmission channel is attention, not income.
insights.quote: That system began to dissolve in 2006 with the launch of the modern social media platforms, accelerated in 2007 with the smartphone and ruptured between 2008 and 2011 with the Great Recession.
insights.locator: That system began to dissolve in 2006

insights.claim: Television concentrated influence among a select few voices while social media re-fragmented it among hundreds of millions, so simple national ideas can no longer hold attention against a feed of identity, grievance, conspiracy and culture war.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Attention economics, not ideology, is the binding constraint on governability — a durable headwind for any policy agenda requiring sustained mass consent.
insights.quote: The shared room of broadcast television became the shouting market of the social network.
insights.locator: Television had concentrated influence

themes.theme: Munich February 2025 as the visible rupture

insights.claim: At the Munich Security Conference on Feb. 14, 2025, JD Vance told European leaders their gravest threat came from within — governments distrusting their own people, courts overturning elections, retreating free speech — and said the U.S. could not defend a civilization that no longer recognized itself.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: The author treats this as the dateable public break in the transatlantic security fiction — a marker for repricing European defense autonomy and alliance-dependent assets.
insights.quote: The United States, he said, could not be expected to defend a civilization that no longer recognized itself.
insights.locator: That was when, at the Munich Security Conference

insights.claim: Hours after Vance, Marco Rubio declared the postwar order over and what comes next transactional and multipolar, and Friedrich Merz — days from becoming German chancellor — responded that Europe could no longer count on Washington, with European editorial pages reaching for the word 'betrayal'.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Documents the elite-level consensus break in real time; the transactional/multipolar framing is the operating assumption to price into trade, defense and alliance exposure.
insights.quote: The postwar order was over; what came next would be transactional and multipolar.
insights.locator: Hours later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio

insights.claim: The belief Vance broke with was the American-built postwar conception of universal citizenship — that rights precede states, that liberal democracy is the only legitimate political form, and that the West is the community holding those convictions in common — a fiction that let 300 million Americans, half a billion Europeans and billions more cooperate as trading partners and allies.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Ties the belief system directly to the scale of the trading bloc: if the fiction fails, the cooperation scale it underwrote — global supply chains, alliance security guarantees — contracts with it.
insights.quote: It is a transcendent frame in the truest sense: a fiction that lets us cooperate beyond our biological limits.
insights.locator: In Munich last year, the transcendent belief

insights.claim: Munich in February 2025 was the moment the restorationist response stopped being an American domestic matter and became a threat to the architecture of the West itself.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Signals that U.S. domestic populism has become an exportable systemic risk to the international order, not a contained electoral cycle.
insights.quote: Munich, in February 2025, was the moment the restorationist response stopped being an American domestic matter and became a threat to the architecture of the West itself.
insights.locator: In the 20th century, proponents of restorationism

insights.claim: Contemporary right-wing populism is structurally restorationist — the same impulse as the ancien régime against the French Revolution, Spanish Carlism and 19th-century clerical-monarchical movements — with MAGA imagining a return to a pre-globalist, more religious, more racially homogeneous nation and European populists from Orbán to Le Pen drawing on related ideas.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Classifies scattered populist movements as one recurring type with a known historical failure mode, which helps forecast their trajectory rather than treating each as sui generis.
insights.quote: Structurally, all are attempts to bring back the god of the tribe.
insights.locator: Maybe because of this uncomfortable truth

insights.claim: The progressive identitarian project that spread through Western universities and institutions over the last decade is a descendant of Jacobinism and Marxism-Leninism — a sacred theory of history, an enlightened vanguard, a project of remaking institutions, and a moral charge against those who resist.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Symmetric indictment of both political poles as backward-looking; useful for reading institutional culture conflicts as structurally equivalent to populism rather than its antidote.
insights.quote: a sacred theory of history (oppression, intersection, liberation), an enlightened vanguard, a project of remaking institutions to align with the theory, and a moral charge against those who resist
insights.locator: The second off-ramp is utopian

insights.claim: In the 20th century restorationism and utopianism — fascism and communism — fought each other for control of states; in the 21st century they fight for control of cultures inside states, so the conflict is no longer over the means of production but over the production of meaning.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Predicts that the contested battleground is institutions, media and platforms rather than territory or industry — locating the risk in cultural infrastructure and content governance.
insights.quote: The conflict is no longer over the means of production; it is over the production of meaning.
insights.locator: In the 20th century, proponents of restorationism

insights.claim: Both off-ramps are anachronisms that reach for yesterday's gods, and neither can answer the real problem — the absence of a stable transcendent framework for 8.3 billion people networked through algorithms, a frame that does not yet exist.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Implies no currently-available political program resolves the instability, so investors should assume prolonged political volatility regardless of which side wins elections.
insights.quote: What neither side will admit is that both off-ramps are anachronisms. Both reach for yesterday’s gods.
insights.locator: What neither side will admit

themes.theme: The interregnum: duration and institutional decay

insights.claim: Historical transitions of this kind take generations: the Reformation required 131 years to settle into the Peace of Westphalia, the Enlightenment needed longer, and the mass media transition produced two world wars and a Cold War before the postwar order stabilized — while the social media transition is still very young.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Sets the time horizon: this is a multi-decade regime, not a cycle to wait out — political-risk premia should be treated as structurally elevated for the foreseeable investment horizon.
insights.quote: The Reformation required 131 years to settle into the Peace of Westphalia.
insights.locator: It may take a long time to emerge

insights.claim: In the gap, institutions still function but with declining legitimacy because they were designed for citizens organized by broadcast; populists rise but cannot build because their proposals are versions of older systems that cannot scale; and intellectuals diagnose but cannot resolve because the resolution requires a transcendent move not yet available.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: A precise description of the current equilibrium — functional-but-illegitimate institutions plus non-constructive challengers — which predicts policy churn and reversal risk rather than durable regime change.
insights.quote: Our institutions still function, but with declining legitimacy, because they were designed for citizens organized by broadcast.
insights.locator: In the meantime, we live in the gap

insights.claim: The new transcendent fiction will likely be assembled not by today's actors but by the next generation growing up inside the new technologies, who will accept as self-evident the conditions current adults find frustrating or untenable.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Generational adoption, not policy design, is the resolution mechanism — a reason to weight cohort behavior on platforms over elite discourse when forecasting long-run political norms.
insights.quote: people who are growing up inside the new technologies and who will accept as self-evident conditions that we find frustrating or even untenable
insights.locator: The new transcendent fiction will likely be assembled

themes.theme: AI as the taming technology and hyper-democracy

insights.claim: Every previous communication-driven disruption was eventually tamed by the same technology that caused it — the press that broke Christendom produced the Enlightenment, the revolutionary newspaper matured into the daily companion of stable 1815-1914 citizen-democracy, and interwar propaganda media matured into the calmer broadcast television conversation of the postwar order.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: The author's most investable pattern: expect the stabilizing solution to come from within the disruptive technology stack, not from regulation that suppresses it.
insights.quote: In each case, what initially fragmented the public sphere is what, in its maturer form, eventually rebuilt it.
insights.locator: There is a pattern here that may give us a reason for hope

insights.claim: If the pattern holds, the social media disruption will be resolved not by abandoning social media but by its next iteration as shaped by artificial intelligence — AI could deepen the chaos but is also the most plausible candidate to eventually tame the disorder.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Frames AI-native social platforms as the structurally important category for the next order — and implies attempts to fix politics by restricting platforms are fighting the wrong battle.
insights.quote: The new transcendent framework, whatever its content, will not arrive in spite of these technologies. It will arrive through them.
insights.locator: If the pattern holds, the disruption caused by social media

insights.claim: We are currently in the chaotic phase that corresponds historically to the Wars of Religion or to the demagogue's radio — that is, the destructive early stage of the media cycle, not the stabilizing mature stage.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Positions the present at the maximum-turbulence point of the analogy, implying conditions get worse before the maturation phase begins.
insights.quote: We are still inside the chaotic phase, the phase that corresponds historically to the Wars of Religion or to the demagogue’s radio.
insights.locator: If the pattern holds, the disruption caused by social media

insights.claim: Social media plus AI open the possibility of hyper-democracy: a platform connecting every person to relevant issues through information, discussion and voting, with AI coordinating inputs from billions of people and translating them into options, goals and strategies to be voted on, shaping policy by influencing Congressional action.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: A concrete, buildable product thesis — AI-mediated mass deliberation infrastructure — that would be the civic-tech category to watch if the pattern-based prediction is right.
insights.quote: The enormous potential of AI to coordinate inputs from billions of people, then translate them into options, goals and strategies to be voted upon … cannot be overestimated.
insights.locator: Social media and AI offer the possibility

insights.claim: The main risk to a hyper-democratic platform is capture — some group controlling it, exactly as happened with which books could be published, which news reached print and, notoriously, the control of mass media.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: Names platform-control concentration as the central governance risk of the next order, which is where regulatory and political conflict should be expected to concentrate.
insights.quote: As always, there is the risk of some group controlling the platform
insights.locator: As always, there is the risk

insights.claim: Across the last 500 years all three communications transformations initially created enormous chaos and expectations of doom yet each ended in a more democratic world — the printing press yielding freedoms of religion, expression and organization; newspapers spreading Liberalism across Europe; mass media enabling Mussolini, Hitler and Stalin but afterward expanding democracy.
insights.speaker: MACARIO SCHETTINO
insights.so_what: The bullish long-arc case: extreme near-term political disorder has historically been compatible with an ultimately wider franchise — an argument against permanently derating democratic systems.
insights.quote: mass media permitted the ascent of autocrats like Mussolini, Hitler and Stalin, but afterward, expanded democracy
insights.locator: Over the last 500 years, three great transformations
